name: Parassinikadavu Sree Muthappan Temple (Parassini Madappura)
tagline: The daily theyyam madappura on the Valapattanam — Muthappan who eats, drinks and answers devotees
summary: Parassinikadavu Sree Muthappan Temple (Parassini Madappura) is a major pilgrimage spot in Kannur, famous for daily Muthappan theyyam, unique non‑Brahminical rituals and the annual Puthari…
description: Parassinikadavu Sree Muthappan Temple (commonly called Parassini Madappura) sits on the banks of the Valapattanam river in Anthoor, Kannur. The presiding deity is Sree Muthappan, a folk manifestation worshipped through ritual theyyam rather than a fixed idol.

The temple matters because its rites break from classical Brahminical temple practice: Muthappan accepts offerings of fish, meat and toddy, a dog is regarded as sacred, and the deity appears as theyyam (Thiruvappana and Vellattam) performed daily in morning and evening sessions.

Visitors get a living ritual experience — predictable daily performances, simple communal prasadam (tea, boiled beans and coconut, and free lunch/dinner at set times) and warm local hospitality with free dormitory-style lodging provided by the madappura during pilgrim stays.

Tradition and legend accompany every visit: the Muthappan story, the hunter‑form of Shiva/Vishnu twin aspects and village harvest customs are shared as oral tradition at the madappura; these are described as local belief rather than historical fact.
highlights: Daily Muthappan theyyam performances (Vellattam and Thiruvappana) — morning and evening
Puthari Thiruvappana harvest festival (early December) — major annual event
Unconventional offerings: fish, meat and toddy; temple prasadam served to the temple dog first
Free communal meals and dormitory accommodation for devotees
Riverside setting on the Valapattanam and easy access from Kannur

sections.heading: Background
body: Parassinikadavu Madappura is a folk shrine dedicated to Sree Muthappan, a popular deity in North Kerala presented through the ritual art of theyyam. The madappura follows local, non‑Brahminical customs and serves as a regional centre for Muthappan worship.
Local tradition links Muthappan to hunter figures and to both Shiva and Vishnu aspects; dogs are sacred at the madappura and feature in rituals and prasadam customs.

sections.heading: What to see and do
body: Attend the theyyam enactments: the minimal Vellattam and the fuller Thiruvappana are presented routinely in the morning and evening. Devotees approach the performer for oral counsel and blessings (this is part of the living ritual tradition).

Taste the temple prasadam and free meals: the madappura serves tea/steamed beans and coconut, with free communal lunch and dinner according to the temple schedule. Walk the riverside compound and observe the madappura’s images, dogs and festival paraphernalia.

sections.heading: Plan your visit
body: Reach the madappura from Kannur (about 20 km) or Taliparamba (about 10 km). Kannur Railway Station and Kannur International Airport provide the nearest long‑distance connections; regular local buses and taxis run to Parassinikadavu.

Check daily theyyam and festival timings before you go. The temple publishes prasadam and meal times and offers free lodging; confirm current schedules and any special arrangements directly with the madappura or DTPC Kannur before travel.

latest.text: Kerala Tourism lists Puthari Thiruvappana (the annual Puthari harvest Thiruvappana) at Parassinikadavu on 2 December 2026; this is the temple's major yearly festival.
Local theyyam listings and temple pages confirm that Muthappan theyyam (Thiruvappana and Vellattam) is performed daily in morning and evening at Parassinikadavu.

visitorInfo.bestTime: Visit any time for daily theyyam; early December for the Puthari Thiruvappana harvest festival.
visitorInfo.howToReach: By road from Kannur (≈20 km) or Taliparamba (≈10 km). Regular buses and taxis serve Parassinikadavu; nearest railhead is Kannur Railway Station and nearest airport is Kannur International Airport (~32 km).
etiquette: Respect temple customs: non‑vegetarian offerings and toddy are part of the ritual — do not treat them as a deviation but as local tradition.
Dogs on the premises are considered sacred; do not disturb or feed them without permission.
Prasadam and free meals follow set times; check the temple website or call before you travel to confirm current meal and darshan timings.
Photography may be sensitive during theyyam and pujas — ask permission from temple staff or performers.
